'''Gene Grabeel''' (June 5, 1920 – January 30, 2015) was an American [[mathematician]] and [[Cryptanalysis|cryptanalyst]] who founded the [[Venona project]].<ref>{{Cite web|last=Benson |first=Robert L.|title=The Venona Story |url=https://www.nsa.gov/Portals/70/documents/about/cryptologic-heritage/historical-figures-publications/publications/coldwar/venona_story.pdf|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190223152318/https://www.nsa.gov/Portals/70/documents/about/cryptologic-heritage/historical-figures-publications/publications/coldwar/venona_story.pdf|archive-date=23 February 2019 |access-date=22 March 2021|publisher=[[National Security Agency]]}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=CI Reader Volume 2 Chapter 4|url= https://fas.org/irp/ops/ci/docs/ci2/2ch4_a.htm |access-date=2021-03-23 |website=fas.org}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Eight New Historical Highway Markers Approved |url=https://www.dhr.virginia.gov/articles-blogs-contributions-in-newsletters/eight-new-historical-highway-markers-approved/|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200320024902/https://www.dhr.virginia.gov/articles-blogs-contributions-in-newsletters/eight-new-historical-highway-markers-approved/|archive-date=20 March 2020|access-date=22 March 2021 |website=[[Virginia Department of Historic Resources]]}}</ref>

== Early life ==
Grabeel was born on June 5, 1920, in [[Rose Hill, Lee County, Virginia]], where she grew up; her mother raised chickens and her father farmed tobacco.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|last=Steber |first=Liza |last2=Mundy |first2=Maggie |title=The Women Code Breakers Who Unmasked Soviet Spies |url=https://www.smithsonianmag.com/history/women-code-breakers-unmasked-soviet-spies-180970034/ |access-date=2021-03-19|website=Smithsonian Magazine|language=en}}</ref> She graduated from [[Mars Hill College]] and [[Farmville State Teachers College]] and initially worked as a high school [[home economics]] teacher in [[Madison Heights, Virginia|Madison Heights]] to teenage girls.<ref name=":0"/><ref name="obit">{{Cite news|date=2015-02-15|title=GRABEEL, GENE|work=[[Richmond Times-Dispatch]] |url=http://www.richmond.com/obituaries/grabeel-gene/article_3d11848c-bd49-5f3e-a5d0-b4439f10aed0.html |access-date=2018-01-17}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite news|last=Dickey |first=Christopher|date=2019-05-26 |title=Brilliant Codebreakers Exposed Soviet Spies—And Launched the McCarthy Era|work=The Daily Beast |language=en |url=https://www.thedailybeast.com/the-brilliant-venona-codebreakers-exposed-soviet-spiesand-launched-the-mccarthy-era|access-date=2021-03-23}}</ref>

== Career ==
On the recommendation of a friend of hers, [[Frank Rowlett]], Grabeel joined the [[Signal Intelligence Service]] on December 28, 1942, where she was assigned to attack intercepted Soviet ciphertext.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" /> Her father gave her his permission to do so and "push some papers around" during the next few months.<ref name=":1" /> Thus Grabeel began her 36-year career with the [[Signal Intelligence Service]].

On February 1, 1943, she founded the [[Venona project]], a counterintelligence program aimed at decrypting Soviet communications.<ref name="codewarriors">{{Cite book|last=Budiansky |first=Stephen |date=2016-06-14 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=KxyeCgAAQBAJ&pg=PA10|title=Code Warriors: NSA's Codebreakers and the Secret Intelligence War Against the Soviet Union|publisher=Knopf Doubleday Publishing Group |isbn=9780385352673 |language=en}}</ref><ref name="codebreaker">{{citation|last=Pincock|first=Stephen |title=Codebreaker: The History of Secret Communication |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=RmOXyoJJKE8C&pg=PA122|page=122|year=2006 |publisher=Bloomsbury|isbn=9780802715470}}</ref><ref name="trib">{{Cite news|last=Kilian |first=Michael|date=1995-07-12|title=50-year Secret: How U.S. Broke Soviet A-bomb Spies' Code |language=en|work=[[Chicago Tribune]] |url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/1995/07/12/50-year-secret-how-us-broke-soviet-a-bomb-spies-code/|access-date=2018-01-17}}</ref><ref name="nsa">{{cite web|last=Benson |first=Robert L.|title=The Venona Story |url=https://www.nsa.gov/about/cryptologic-heritage/historical-figures-publications/publications/coldwar/assets/files/venona_story.pdf|access-date=2018-01-18|website=[[National Security Agency]]}}</ref> She and others spent months sifting through stored and incoming Soviet telegrams.<ref name="cia">{{cite web|date=19 March 2007|title=Venona: Soviet Espionage and The American Response 1939-1957 -- Preface|url=https://www.cia.gov/library/center-for-the-study-of-intelligence/csi-publications/books-and-monographs/venona-soviet-espionage-and-the-american-response-1939-1957/preface.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070613142151/https://www.cia.gov/library/center-for-the-study-of-intelligence/csi-publications/books-and-monographs/venona-soviet-espionage-and-the-american-response-1939-1957/preface.htm|archive-date=13 June 2007|url-status=dead|access-date=2018-01-18|website=[[Central Intelligence Agency]]}}</ref> Grabeel initially worked with [[Leonard Zubko]], a Russian speaker, but he was soon replaced.<ref name=":0" />

In his book ''Code Warriors: NSA's Codebreakers and the Secret Intelligence War Against the Soviet Union'', [[Stephen Budiansky]] describes how she came into the opportunity to work as a U.S. government cryptanalyst:
{{Blockquote
|text=Gene Grabeel ... was teaching high school near [[Lynchburg, Virginia|Lynchburg]] in central Virginia and dissatisfied with her job when she met a young Army officer in the post office who was looking for college graduates to go work at an undisclosed location near Washington, to do a job he could not offer any details about. ... Grabeel had been thinking about trying to get a job with the federal government and asked her father what he thought of the idea. He told her she might as well "go to Washington for six months and shuffle papers." She was off to the capital as soon as she found a replacement teacher to take over for her.
|author=Stephen Budiansky
(2016)<ref name=codewarriors/>
}}Grabeel retired from service in 1978, as the [[Venona project]] came to a close.<ref name=":0" />

== Personal life ==
Grabeel attended Blackstone Baptist Church.
She was a member of the [[Daughters of the American Revolution]] and of the 17th Century Colonial Dames.<ref name=obit/> Later in life, she was a fan of [[University of Virginia]] basketball.<ref name=":0" /> She dated men, but was not interested in marriage, similarly to her colleagues.<ref name=":0" />

== Death and legacy ==
Grabeel died at age 94 on January 30, 2015, in [[Blackstone, Virginia]].
<ref name="obit" /> After the 1995 [[Classified information in the United States#Declassification|declassification]] of the Venona project, Grabeel was recognized by the [[Central Intelligence Agency]] as an "American Hero".
<ref name="obit" /> She was memorialized with a historical highway marker along with [[Frank Rowlett]] in Virginia.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Still|first=Mike|title=Rose Hill natives honored for decades of codebreaking, cryptographic work|url=https://www.timesnews.net/news/local-news/rose-hill-natives-honored-for-decades-of-codebreaking-cryptographic-work/article_b1db71b6-4ec4-59ed-bc8c-d9532c2dfe88.html|access-date=2021-03-21|website=timesnews.net|language=en}}</ref>
